label: Codex Atlanticus
summary: Collection of 1119 sheets of Leonardo's drawings and writings assembled by Pompeo Leoni in the late sixteenth century, held by the Veneranda Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Milan.
history: Orazio Melzi and dispersal after Francesco Melzi's death
Pompeo Leoni, assembly late sixteenth century

claims.statement: The codex now consists of 1119 sheets, the count after the twentieth century restoration.

sources.cite: Veneranda Biblioteca Ambrosiana on Google Arts and Culture, Ten key facts about Leonardo da Vinci's Codex Atlanticus.

check_in: Ambrosiana official description

claims.statement: The sheets are dated individually across Leonardo's whole working life, c.1478 to 1519. The span is an aggregate of sheet datings, not a date of the codex as a unit.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Codex Atlanticus (background only, not grounds).

check_in: Pedretti 1978 to 1979, The Codex Atlanticus: A Catalogue of Its Newly Restored Sheets

claims.statement: Pedretti's catalogue of the restored sheets assigns a date to each sheet; it is the standard chronology of the codex. Individual sheet datings must be taken from it and recorded on the sheet or the work drawn on it, never from this record.
check_in: Pedretti 1978 to 1979, The Codex Atlanticus: A Catalogue of Its Newly Restored Sheets

value.text: Assembled by Pompeo Leoni, late sixteenth century

claims.statement: Pompeo Leoni formed the codex by cutting and mounting sheets from Leonardo's papers, including sheets taken from original notebooks, in a large album.

value.text: Leoni obtained the Melzi papers between 1582 and 1590

claims.statement: Leoni is said to have obtained the papers from Orazio Melzi after his return from Spain in 1582 and by 1590, the year of Lomazzo's mention; another account says he took seven volumes plus three bought from Mazenta to Spain in 1590.

value.text: Donated to the Ambrosiana by deed of 21 January 1637

claims.statement: Galeazzo Arconati gave the codex with other Leonardo volumes (twelve volumes in the printed instrument of donation) to the Biblioteca Ambrosiana; a recent study of the original deed dates it 21 January 1637, executed through the proxy Cristoforo Sola.

sources.cite: Marcuccio, Roberto, article on the Arconati donation deed to the Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Achademia Leonardi Vinci, n.s., 2022 (only the opening pages were seen in a search result: deed dated 21 January 1637, executed through the proxy Cristoforo Sola).

claims.statement: The codex was removed from the Ambrosiana to Paris by the French after Bonaparte's entry into Milan in 1796. One source gives 1795.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Codex Atlanticus (background only, not grounds).

claims.statement: After the Congress of Vienna ordered restitution in 1815, the Codex Atlanticus alone returned to the Ambrosiana; the other Leonardo manuscripts taken in 1796 stayed in Paris at the Institut de France.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Codex Atlanticus (background only, not grounds).

value.text: Restored at the Abbey of Grottaferrata, 1962 to 1972

claims.statement: The sheets were detached from Leoni's album and remounted in 12 volumes by the Laboratorio del Libro Antico of the Abbey of Grottaferrata; Italian reports give 1962 to 1972, English sources 1968 to 1972.

value.text: Volumes disbound for rotating display from 2008 to 2009

claims.statement: The twelve volumes were taken apart and the sheets have been shown in rotation at the Ambrosiana and in the Bramante Sacristy of Santa Maria delle Grazie since 2009.

sources.cite: Varesenews, The long story of the Atlantic Code, November 2009.

value.text: Stains caused by mercury salts and sulphur

claims.statement: A Politecnico di Milano study (Scientific Reports, 2023) traced stains on the sheets to mercury salts from earlier conservation and sulphur from pollution.

sources.cite: ANSA, Culprits behind stains on Leonardo's Codex Atlanticus found, 9 May 2023.

claims.statement: Digital reconstruction of the Codex Atlanticus published by Museo Galileo with the Ambrosiana, Royal Collection Trust and Biblioteca Leonardiana in March 2023; version 2.0 launched in London on 8 June 2026 digitally reinserts about 550 sheets cut out in the sixteenth century.
